title: Analyst
headline: Answer questions with SQL in Studio
persona: You write queries and want answers. Someone else worries about tables, tokens and pipelines.
outcomes: Find your way around Opteryx Studio and the public sample datasets
Write SELECT queries with filters, joins, aggregates and window functions
Read an execution plan and say why a query is slow or expensive
Pull Opteryx data into Excel or Power BI over OData
prerequisites: An account on opteryx.app. Any Google, Microsoft or GitHub login works.
Some SQL. The path teaches the Opteryx dialect, not SQL from scratch.

steps.title: What is Opteryx
steps.why: Where the engine fits and what it is not, so the rest of the path has context.

steps.title: Logging in
steps.why: Sign in with a provider you already have. There is nothing to install.

steps.title: Site tour
steps.why: The catalog, editor, results and reference panels you will spend the rest of the path in.

steps.title: Load and query data
steps.why: The public datasets you can query without loading anything, and the three ways to read data back.

steps.title: SQL introduction
steps.why: A tutorial on the query language: relations, projection, filtering, joins and aggregation.

steps.title: SELECT
steps.why: The full statement shape, clause by clause, in the order the engine applies them.

steps.title: JOIN
steps.why: Every join type Opteryx supports, including the ones that answer which rows have no match.

steps.title: Aggregates
steps.why: The functions that turn many rows into one, and how each treats NULL.

steps.title: Window functions
steps.why: Rankings and running totals without collapsing rows.

steps.title: Working with timestamps
steps.why: Dates are where most analyst SQL goes wrong. Extraction, truncation and arithmetic.

steps.title: Troubleshooting queries
steps.why: EXPLAIN, and the handful of changes that fix most slow queries.

steps.title: Cost model
steps.why: What a query costs and why selecting fewer columns is cheaper.

steps.title: Querying via OData
steps.why: Read Opteryx tables from Excel or Power BI with no code.

title: Data engineer
headline: Build tables that maintain themselves
persona: You own the tables other people query: loading them, shaping them, keeping them fresh and controlling who sees what.
outcomes: Load files into catalog tables from the UI, the API or the command line
Create, change and compact tables, and read any earlier version of them
Replace a refresh pipeline with a materialized view, or with a task and a trigger
Grant access with roles and know what each role permits
Point a workspace at your own Iceberg catalog
prerequisites: The Analyst path, or comfort with SQL DDL and DML.

steps.title: When to use Opteryx
steps.why: Where it fits and where it does not, before you design around it.

steps.title: Load and query data
steps.why: The upload session, part and commit flow that every ingestion path uses.

steps.why: A full round trip: CTAS, UPDATE, DELETE, snapshots, OPTIMIZE and DROP.

steps.title: INSERT
steps.why: Append rows from literal values or from a query.

steps.title: MERGE
steps.why: Upserts: the statement behind most incremental loads.

steps.title: Time travel queries
steps.why: Read a table as it was at a snapshot or at a point in time.

steps.title: When a materialized view replaces a pipeline
steps.why: One statement instead of a scheduler, a job and a swap. And when that is the wrong trade.

steps.title: CREATE TRIGGER
steps.why: Wire a task to a table, and whose identity an unattended run carries.

steps.why: Workspaces as the boundary, and what reader, writer and owner each allow.

steps.title: Federator

steps.why: Keep your tables in your own Iceberg REST catalog instead of Opteryx storage.

steps.title: Cost model
steps.why: How usage is measured, so refresh frequency and scan width are deliberate choices.

title: Developer
headline: Call Opteryx from your own code
persona: You are wiring Opteryx into an application, a notebook or a service, and you need auth, a client and a result you can work with.
outcomes: Authenticate with client credentials, and without any stored secret using OIDC
Submit SQL over HTTP and turn the columnar result into rows
Query from Python through SQLAlchemy, pandas and Arrow Flight SQL
Embed the engine in your own process and query local Parquet
prerequisites: An account on opteryx.app for the hosted parts. The embedded engine needs only pip.
